bib.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; transfer-matrix numbers (Fig 2, Fig 9) are heatmap cell values, not read individually; Figure 5 prefix text is an image and not in the text layer.

question: Can a language model's latent knowledge of truth be recovered from its unlabeled hidden activations alone, without labels or model outputs?
hypothesis: Truth satisfies logical consistency properties (a statement and its negation have opposite truth values) that few other features satisfy, so a direction enforcing them will recover truth.
contributions: Contrast-Consistent Search (CCS), an unsupervised probe that finds a direction in activation space consistent across negations
CCS outperforms calibrated zero-shot on 6 models and 10 datasets and halves prompt sensitivity
CCS stays accurate under a misleading prefix, transfers across tasks, and works with little data
Contrastive Representation Clustering (TPC, BSS) shows truth directions are salient

method.summary: For each yes-no question build two statements (answered Yes, answered No), extract last-token hidden states, mean-normalise each set independently, and train a linear+sigmoid probe with a consistency loss plus a confidence loss. No labels and no model outputs are used; model weights are frozen.
method.task: binary (yes-no) question answering / classification via unsupervised probing of hidden states

datasets.name: IMDB, Amazon (sentiment); AG-News, DBpedia-14 (topic); RTE, QNLI (NLI); COPA, Story-Cloze (story completion); BoolQ (QA); PIQA (commonsense)
datasets.size: 1000 examples per dataset, label-balanced (COPA 500 total); about 180k examples counting 9 prompts x 10 datasets x 6 models
datasets.source: public datasets; test/validation split used when possible, else some train examples
datasets.preprocessing: each converted to a binary task; for AG-News and DBpedia a random incorrect label is paired with the correct one, randomly assigned to label0/label1

datasets.name: MNLI
datasets.source: used to finetune RoBERTa and DeBERTa for the zero-shot baseline (Yin et al. 2020)

models.name: DeBERTa (v2)
models.init_from: finetuned on MNLI (not for Appendix C MLM test)

other.note: trained on 9 of the 10 evaluation datasets (all but RTE), excluded from means

training.objective: L_CCS = mean_i [ (p(x+_i) - (1 - p(x-_i)))^2 + min{p(x+_i), p(x-_i)}^2 ]; probe p = sigmoid(theta^T phi~ + b)
training.seeds: 10 random restarts (theta initialised random unit norm); run with lowest unsupervised loss kept

other.what_is_trained: only a linear probe on frozen hidden states; model weights unchanged
other.normalisation: subtract mean of x+ and of x- features separately; also divide by average norm times sqrt(d)
other.hidden_state: last token, last layer unless stated; for encoder-decoder, whichever of encoder/decoder gives lower unsupervised loss
other.prompts_per_dataset: 8 to 13 (9 on average), pooled in one training set, normalised independently per prompt
other.label_direction: evaluation takes the max accuracy over the two possible labelings of the clusters
other.BSS: T = E = 20, Adam, lr 0.1, loss = (var of negative side + var of nonnegative side) / total var

inference.samples: accuracy averaged over about 9 prompts per dataset, 10 datasets, 5 models (T0 excluded); sample-size study resamples k points 32 times
inference.prompting: zero-shot prompts derived or slightly modified from Sanh et al. 2021 (T0/promptsource); x+ and x- = same prompt with the two labels; no few-shot examples except the misleading prefix test

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of the 40% test split classified correctly, averaged over prompts and datasets

metrics.name: prompt sensitivity
metrics.definition: std of accuracy across prompts per model and dataset, averaged over datasets (shown in parentheses)

baselines: zero-shot (highest log prob, averaged over label tokens)
calibrated zero-shot (threshold gamma so predictions are 50/50)
logistic regression on (phi~(x+), phi~(x-)) as supervised ceiling
eval.protocol: Wald test with upper-bound standard error 0.5/sqrt(3800) about 0.8%; main comparisons significant at 0.00001 level. No seeds beyond the 10 restarts.

availability.data: public datasets listed; prompts in Appendix I

prompts.text: x+ = [prefix] Q: Is the sentiment of "[text]" [label0] or [label1]? A: [label0]; x- = same with A: [label1]

prompts.purpose: MLM test with label in the middle of the prompt
prompts.text: The following movie review expresses a [label] sentiment:\n[text]
[prefix]Consider the following example: ''' [text] ''' Choice 1: [label0]. Choice 2: [label1].Between choice 1 and choice 2, the topic of this example is [label]

evidence.quote: we optimize it 10 times using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) with learning rate 0.01
we train each time for E = 1000 epochs with a learning rate η = 0.01

results.claim: CCS beats calibrated zero-shot on average over 5 models (T0 excluded).
results.setup: 10 datasets, about 9 prompts each, models RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-J, T5, UnifiedQA; last-layer last-token states; 1000 examples per dataset, 40% test
results.quote: CCS attains an accuracy of 71.2% on average, compared to 67.2% for calibrated zero-shot.

results.claim: CCS halves prompt sensitivity relative to calibrated zero-shot.
results.metric: mean std of accuracy across prompts
results.table: Table 1, row CCS vs Calibrated 0-shot, column Mean* (3.2 vs 6.1)
results.note: abstract says 'cuts prompt sensitivity in half'

results.claim: Supervised logistic regression ceiling on the same hidden states.
results.note: gap of about 12 points to CCS remains

results.claim: A misleading few-shot prefix drops UnifiedQA zero-shot accuracy but not CCS.
results.setup: UnifiedQA, 10 datasets, prefix of incorrectly answered questions (Fig 5); CCS 82.1 -> 83.8, calibrated 0-shot 80.4 -> 70.9
results.note: Appendix B authors concede results are qualitatively similar with correct-answer prefixes, so the effect may be out-of-distribution rather than imitation of errors

results.claim: CCS on MLM-only DeBERTa with the label mid-prompt and no [MASK] still works, while zero-shot does not.
results.setup: DeBERTa-v2 without NLI finetuning, Amazon, 1000 new points, 60/40 split

results.claim: Training CCS on all datasets together adds an insignificant gain on average, but large for T0.
results.quote: with large gains for T0 in particular (77.6% →84.8%)

results.claim: CCS is worse than zero-shot on RoBERTa and on T0 (whose zero-shot is inflated by training on the test datasets).
results.setup: T0 trained on 9 of 10 evaluation datasets

results.claim: CRC variants (no training of a probe beyond PCA/clustering) are nearly as good as CCS.
Using the encoder vs decoder states for UnifiedQA under the misleading prefix: decoder accuracy falls like zero-shot.
results.metric: CCS accuracy on UnifiedQA decoder states
results.quote: accuracy using the decoder hidden states drops from 81.0% to 73.5%

results.claim: Calibration raises zero-shot accuracy by about 5% on average.
results.quote: We find this increases accuracy by about 5% on average.

results.claim: Training CCS on Amazon transfers with average accuracy slightly above the no-transfer setting.
results.setup: UnifiedQA etc., train on Amazon, test on all datasets
results.quote: achieves an average transfer accuracy of 71.8%, which is 0.6% higher than CCS without transfer

limits: CCS needs a direction that separates true from false and the model must actively evaluate truth; the authors say it is not clear when this holds (Section 5.1).
No test on active lying or deception by models; no such evaluation setup existed (Section 5.1).

CCS does not say which cluster is true; evaluation takes the max over both labelings, so reported accuracy is optimistic by that choice (Section 2.2); Appendix A only sketches an unsupervised fix using conjunctions.
Only yes-no or binary tasks with clear-cut answers; a gap to the LR ceiling remains.
Misleading-prefix effect is ambiguous: qualitatively similar with correct answers, and only UnifiedQA showed a significant drop (Appendix B).
T0 contaminated by training on 9 of 10 datasets; UnifiedQA trained on BoolQ.
Several models (RoBERTa, GPT-J, T5) show weak transfer and near-chance accuracy on some datasets (Fig 9).
Model sizes are not stated; results are for 2020-2021 era models, later work questioned whether CCS finds truth rather than other salient features (not in this paper).

terms.definition: a method that learns a linear projection of the hidden states that is consistent across negations
for each question q_i, the statement x+ answering Yes and x- answering No
cluster the differences of normalized hidden states of contrast pairs, via top principal component (TPC) or bimodal salience search (BSS)
